original_question: A proper vertex coloring is called a 2-homogeneous coloring when exactly 2 colors appear in the open neighborhood of every vertex. If a cubic graph admits a 2-homogeneous coloring, are 4 colors always sufficient?
target_in_paper: Section 5, Problem 5.1 in the subsection "Homogeneous coloring of cubic graphs": "If a cubic graph admits a 2-homogeneous coloring, then 4 colors are always sufficient." The immediately preceding paragraph defines a k-homogeneous coloring as a proper vertex coloring in which exactly k colors appear in the open neighborhood of every vertex. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.02892))
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the paper’s intended target almost exactly: it uses the correct notion of a 2-homogeneous coloring, the correct graph class (cubic graphs), and the correct 4-color sufficiency question. In substance, it is already a near-verbatim restatement of Problem 5.1. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.02892))
missing_details: To be fully stand-alone, make explicit that "4 colors are always sufficient" means: whenever a cubic graph G has some 2-homogeneous coloring, G also has a 2-homogeneous coloring using at most 4 colors. It does not mean merely that G is properly 4-colorable. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.02892))
If you want complete self-containment, specify that a cubic graph is a 3-regular graph. This is standard terminology and implicit in the paper. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.02892))

It helps to write the neighborhood condition in explicit quantifier form, e.g. for every vertex v, the set of colors on N(v) has size exactly 2. The paper states this definition immediately before Problem 5.1. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.02892))

Do not add extra restrictions such as bipartite, connected, or bridgeless. Problem 5.1 is stated for cubic graphs in general; the paper mentions the bipartite case only as an earlier weaker version from the literature. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.02892))
refined_question: Let G be a cubic graph (that is, a 3-regular graph). A proper vertex coloring c of G is called 2-homogeneous if for every vertex v in V(G), exactly two distinct colors appear on the open neighborhood N(v), i.e. |{c(u) : u in N(v)}| = 2. If G admits a 2-homogeneous coloring, must G admit a 2-homogeneous coloring with at most 4 colors? ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.02892))
justification: The draft is aiming at the first of the two open problems posed in Section 5. The surrounding text first defines k-homogeneous coloring, then narrows attention to cubic graphs and asks for the minimum number of colors sufficient among those cubic graphs that admit a 2-homogeneous coloring; Problem 5.1 is exactly the resulting 4-color question. The sentence after Problem 5.2 further confirms that the paper’s intended scope is broader than the earlier bipartite-only version, so the refined question should not insert a bipartite hypothesis. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.02892))

citations.label: Note after Problem 5.2 on the earlier weaker bipartite version
